sections.skill: Check whether a citation exists and supports the claim

questions.prompt: What is an invented citation?

choices.text: A real source that disagrees with the claim
A reference to a source that does not exist
A source that is more than ten years old
A source written by a famous scientist

questions.correct_answer: A reference to a source that does not exist
questions.intro: Citations can be wrong in two different ways. An INVENTED citation points to a source that does not exist: a made-up article, a fake court case, a book with the wrong author. A MISMATCHED citation points to a real source that does NOT support the claim: the article exists, but it says something different, or nothing on the topic. To check, first confirm the source exists (search a library catalog, an official database or the publisher's site), then open it and find the passage that supports the exact claim. In 2023 a federal court in New York sanctioned lawyers who filed court cases invented by a chatbot without checking them.
questions.feedback: Invented means the source is not real.

sections.skill: Separate an assertion from a supporting source

questions.prompt: Which is a supporting source?

choices.text: A named survey report you can open
"It is well known by everyone"
"Experts agree on this point"
"Research shows it clearly"

questions.correct_answer: A named survey report you can open
questions.intro: An ASSERTION is a statement that something is true: "Bananas are the most popular fruit." A SUPPORTING SOURCE is something you can open that shows evidence for it: a survey report with the numbers. Words like "according to experts" or "research shows" are part of the assertion, not a source, unless they name something specific you can find. To separate them, ask: "Is there a specific document or record named here that I could open?" If not, you only have an assertion.
questions.feedback: A specific document can be opened.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Catch citations that exist but do not support the claim

questions.prompt: A source studied adults, but the answer cites it for a claim about children. What is the problem?

choices.text: Studies about adults are always wrong
The source does not support claims about children
None; adults and children respond the same way
The source must be invented

questions.correct_answer: The source does not support claims about children
questions.intro: Checking a citation means comparing the claim with what the source actually says. Watch for small shifts: a study about adults cited for children, a 2015 figure presented as current, a "may help" turned into "cures," or one example presented as a general rule. Also notice WHO the source is: a press release, an opinion piece or an unknown website is weaker support than an original study or an official record. If you cannot find the supporting passage, treat the claim as unsupported, even if the source is real and reputable.
